## GPT-6 Model Family Overview

GPT-6 is OpenAI's family of AI models released in September 2026, made up of GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Sol, and GPT-6 Luna. Astra is the most capable, the Sol models balance ability and cost, and Luna is the cheapest and fastest.

## GPT-6.1 Sol as Default in Codex

On September 29 GPT-6.1 Sol became the default in Codex's bundled model catalog. OpenAI announced GPT-6.1 Sol at DevDay on September 29, describing it as a major upgrade to GPT-6 Sol for agentic coding, priced at one-fifth of GPT-6 Astra's standard rates.

## Model Specifications

GPT-6.1 Sol has a model ID of gpt-6.1-sol, a context window of 1,050,000 tokens with up to 128,000 output tokens, and reasoning effort options from low to max. It's the new middle model of the GPT-6 family, and OpenAI says it nearly matches GPT-6 Astra on agentic coding, computer use and professional work, at a fifth of Astra's price.

## Availability

GPT-6.1 Sol is available to all Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex, and OpenAI's launch page states that it "is not yet available in Chat."

content.content:
A `reasoning_extraction` refusal usually comes from a prompt that asks the model to put its thinking or reasoning in the output, either verbatim or in a fixed format. Common examples:

* A `<thinking>`, `<reasoning>`, or scratchpad section that the model fills in before it answers
* A `reasoning`, `thinking`, or `trace` field in JSON output or in a tool input
* The model's private notes, or a running log of its reasoning
* Reasoning asked for verbatim or in full

The wording can sit in a system prompt, a skill, or a tool description, so check those too.

You can still ask Claude to explain its answer. Ask for a short explanation, the evidence behind a result, or a summary of the actions it took. To see how the model reasoned, set `display: "summarized"` and read the [`thinking` blocks](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/thinking#summarized-thinking). A `reasoning_extraction` refusal usually comes from a prompt that asks the model to put its thinking or reasoning in the output, either verbatim or in a fixed format. Common examples:

* A `<thinking>`, `<reasoning>`, or scratchpad section that the model fills in before it answers

[Effort](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort) is the main control for how much Claude Haiku 5.5 thinks. It replaces the thinking budget (`budget_tokens`) that Claude Haiku 4.5 used, so there's no old setting to carry over. Compare two or three of these levels on your own evals:

* `low` is the cheapest and fastest level. Use it for chat, short tool tasks, and simple, high-volume requests. In long agent prompts, the model is more likely to skip a search, stop early, or skip a check at this level.
* `medium` is the default. Start here for most work, including agentic coding.
* `high` suits knowledge work, longer agent tasks, and strict instruction following.
* `xhigh` and `max` are for work where a quality gain on your evals justifies the cost. Thinking and replies get much longer at these levels, so also run your evals on Claude Sonnet 5.5 and compare performance, cost, and speed.

Claude Haiku 5.5 is the first Haiku model with effort levels. Thinking works as follows:
Start at the default [effort](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort) level, `high`, then test the other levels (`low`, `medium`, `xhigh`, and `max`) against your own evals. Effort is the primary control for trading off intelligence, latency, and cost on Claude Fable 5.1. Re-run the sweep even if you already ran one on Claude Fable 5: effort level names don't correspond to the same amount of thinking across models.

Claude Fable 5.1's capability gains over Claude Fable 5 show up across effort levels and are largest at the higher settings. At `medium`, results roughly match Claude Fable 5 at lower cost, so step down to `medium` or `low` where your evals show quality holds. At `low`, Claude Fable 5.1 is often competitive with Claude Opus and Claude Sonnet models on cost per task while scoring higher, so include it in the comparison wherever you'd otherwise run a smaller model at a higher effort level.

Two effort-specific behaviors have their own sections: at `low`, Claude Fable 5.1 calls search and retrieval tools less often (see [Search triggering at low effort](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-fable-5-1#search-triggering-at-low-effort)), and at `xhigh` and `max` it can think for longer before writing a long deliverable (see [Leave room for long outputs at xhigh and max effort](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-fable-5-1#leave-room-for-long-outputs-at-xhigh-and-max-effort)).

prompting-claude-fable-5.md:115:In very long sessions, Claude Fable 5 can occasionally suggest a new session, offer to summarize and hand off, or trim its own work. This is most often triggered when the harness shows a remaining-token countdown to the model. Avoid surfacing explicit context-budget counts where possible. If the harness must show them, a reassurance helps:
prompting-claude-fable-5.md:173:* **Make self-verification explicit in long-run prompts.** Separate, fresh-context verifier subagents tend to outperform self-critique. For long-running tasks, instruct: `Establish a method for checking your own work at an interval of [X] as you build. Run this every [X interval], verifying your work with subagents against the specification.`
## Verification on coding tasks

On agentic coding tasks, Claude Sonnet 5.5 generally checks its work before it reports a change as done. At `low` effort, though, it sometimes reports a change as done without running a check that exercises it. For example, it might skip the project's tests because the project's dependencies aren't installed.

If you see changes reported as complete without test or build output in the transcript, add this paragraph, or one like it, to the system prompt. At `low` effort, it makes skipped or superficial checks rare, with no measurable change in task quality and only a slightly higher cost per task:

```text wrap
* Replies in a chat application start slowly because the model thinks at length first: [Thinking instructions in chat system prompts](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-opus-5-5#thinking-instructions-in-chat-system-prompts)
* The model follows instructions that arrived inside text a user pasted: [Mark pasted text in user messages](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-opus-5-5#mark-pasted-text-in-user-messages)
* Answers about dense charts, diagrams, or screenshots miss detail: [Tools for complex visual inputs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-opus-5-5#tools-for-complex-visual-inputs)
* Frontend output looks generic: [Frontend design defaults](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-opus-5-5#frontend-design-defaults)

## CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH

The `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` environment variable controls the default limit of 3 layers of subagents below your main conversation.

### How It Works

Claude Code counts layers of subagents below your main conversation. Agents spawned directly from your session are the first layer, and each generation below adds one. At the default of 3, a subagent on the third layer cannot spawn further, so it does its delegated work itself.

### Version History

In v2.1.217 through v2.1.218, the limit defaulted to one, so a subagent couldn't spawn its own unless you raised it; v2.1.219 raised the default to three.

### Configuration

The variable needs Claude Code v2.1.217 or later and accepts a positive whole number, so you can adjust the limit but not remove it. To disable nesting entirely, you can set it to 1.

### Related Limits

There are two other related environment variables:
- `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS` (default 20, since v2.1.217) and `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENTS_PER_SESSION` (default 200, since v2.1.212)

Custom agents Codex ships with built-in agents: default : general-purpose fallback agent. worker : execution-focused agent for implementation and fixes. explorer : read-heavy codebase exploration agent. To define your own custom agents, add standalone TOML files under ~/.codex/agents/ for personal agents or .codex/agents/ for project-scoped agents. Each file defines one custom agent. Custom agents can change model settings and instructions or disable supported capabilities. They inherit the parent’s permissions, provider, and MCP servers; a custom agent file can’t override those settings. Every standalone custom agent file must define: name description developer_instructions If a custom agent file sets model or model_reasoning_effort , the value in the file takes precedence. Before applying the file, Codex resolves each setting from an explicit spawn value, then the corresponding [agents] default, then the parent’s value. If an explicit spawn request or an [agents] default selects a model and neither supplies a reasoning effort, Codex uses that model’s default effort. A custom agent file that sets only model preserves this previously resolved effort. Set model_reasoning_effort in the file too if the selected model doesn’t support that effort or you want a different one. Skills inherit from the parent, and a custom agent can disable individual skills with skills.config . Global settings Global subagent settings still live under [agents] in your configuration . Field Type Required Purpose agents.enabled boolean No Enable or disable multi-agent tools. agents.max_concurrent_threads_per_session number No Cap concurrently open spawned-agent threads, excluding the primary. agents.default_subagent_model string No Set the default model for spawned agents. agents.default_subagent

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Vercel's design.md design agent:

## The 57% Failure Reduction

Vercel published design.md, which cut agent-generated design failures by 57%. In three desktop scenarios, when testing with GPT-5.5, Vercel's deterministic checks counted 39 instances of known failure modes with design.md, compared to 91 without it.

## Testing Methodology

Vercel tested every iteration against a repeatable set of seven evaluation prompts, designed to expose how changes in guidance ultimately affected the generated output. Three scenarios for desktop were selected, and each was generated twice using Codex (GPT-5.5) — once with design.md loaded and once without. Only the first generation of each was adopted, with no retries. A deterministic check was run on a total of 6 pages to count how many known failures occur.

## Important Limitations

After more than 200 runs refining the system, not one of the six tested pages was ready to ship without correction. Encoding human judgment into reusable agent guidance can help reduce recurring failures, but it's no silver bullet.

The design.md system combines three components: the markdown guidance file itself, a public stylesheet with CSS classes and design tokens, and an evaluation loop using both deterministic checks and human review.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about uSpec:

## Overview

uSpec is an agentic system that connects an AI agent in Cursor to Figma through the open-source Figma Console MCP. Uber's design systems team uses AI agents and Figma Console MCP to generate up-to-date component specs in minutes instead of weeks.

## How It Works

Two layers work together: agent skills that carry the spec-writing expertise, and an MCP bridge that gives the agent direct read-write access to your Figma file.

### Agent Skills

Each skill loads its own instruction file with validation rules, structured schemas, and reference documentation. The screen reader skill, for example, loads platform-specific accessibility property references (VoiceOver modifiers, TalkBack semantics, ARIA roles) before analyzing the component.

## Data Integration

The agent reads real data from your Figma file, with token names, variant axes, variable modes, and component properties coming directly from your design system.

## Project Overview

uSpec generates design system documentation for UI components directly from an AI agent, rendering into Figma or a portable .md file. It works with Figma Console MCP or the native Figma MCP, inside Cursor, Claude Code, or Codex.

## Repository Details

The uSpec repository is maintained by redongreen on GitHub and contains folders for figma-plugin and skills. uSpec captures component specifications with the uSpec Extract Figma plugin, compiles a canonical component contract (.json) plus a portable implementation guide (.md), then renders sections of that specification back into Figma as annotation frames.

## Skills Repository

There are 11 skills available in the GitHub repository that can be installed for Claude Code, ChatGPT, and Codex via npx skills add redongreen/uSpec. The skills generate design system documentation covering API properties, structure, color tokens, anatomy, motion, and screen-reader behavior.

The project is licensed under MIT v2.4.0.

There's also a related project called Figma Console MCP Skills that repackages Figma Console MCP capabilities as Markdown skills for the native Figma MCP server, providing token export/import, variable management, component-set analysis, WCAG linting, accessibility audits, and other design-systems capabilities.

# Code Connect Impact Metrics

## Key Results

Based on Figma's evaluation of Code Connect in their MCP server:

**Median improvements with Code Connect enabled:**
- **Code Quality**: +1 point on a 1–4 Likert scale (from 2 to 3)
- **Token Usage**: -29.5% reduction
- **Task Duration**: -19.6% reduction

## Study Details

The evaluation tested 27 design-to-code tasks across two React-based design systems:
- Simple Design System (SDS) with ~20% Code Connect coverage
- Figma Pattern Library (FPL) with ~6% Code Connect coverage

Tom Weightman, the Software Engineer who authored the analysis, notes: "When Code Connect coverage is high, agents tend to make fewer exploratory tool calls and spend less time grepping for component and icon names."

## Coinbase Case Study

Frontend Engineer Erich Kuerschner from Coinbase's Design Systems team observed that "without Code Connect, the agent would sometimes fabricate its own version of components" but with it enabled, "the output code quality vastly improved and we saved tokens."

The specific percentages you referenced (11.5%/22.3%/22.5%) do not appear in the provided article content.

## State of AI in Design Systems Survey (July 2026)

The "State of AI in Design Systems" is a field survey from July 2026 of how 21 actively maintained open-source design systems make themselves legible to machines, plus the six platforms around them.

**Survey Scope:**
The survey was conducted by Kaelig Deloumeau-Prigent, co-chair of the W3C Design Tokens Community Group, who audited 20 open-source design systems and 6 platforms, logging 187 AI affordances and 157 techniques.

**Key Affordances Found:**
The most common affordances include: MCP server (20), Agent skill (19), Repo agent files (16), llms.txt (15), AI docs (15), Storybook (14), Registry (11), Editor rules (9), CLI (9), and Code Connect (3).

**Major Finding:**
The overwhelming finding is absence: almost none of the surveyed systems have llms.txt, Code Connect, or agent instruction files, and several that appear to serve llms.txt actually return 404s or HTML shells disguised as 200 responses.

The full survey is available at https://state-of-ai-in-design-systems.netlify.app with markdown twins, JSON exports, and an MCP server for querying the data.

# State of AI in Design Systems — July 2026: Key Findings

## Headline Statistics

The study examined **21 design systems across 6 platforms**, identifying **200 AI affordances and 165 coercion techniques**. Data collection occurred July 26-28, 2026, with publication September 21, 2026.

## Distribution of AI Capabilities

Among the systems analyzed:
- **20 of 21** systems implemented at least one MCP server
- **15 of 21** shipped `llms.txt` files
- **19 of 21** included agent skills (Claude-native integrations)
- **14 of 21** provided Storybook integration

## Maturity Classification

The systems stratified into three tiers:
- **15 systems** classified as "ai-native"
- **5 systems** marked as "invested"
- **1 system** designated "emerging"

## Important Context

The authors emphasize this represents "a dated snapshot, not a live index" and caution that "what design systems ship for agents changed a lot during 2026." They recommend consulting individual system records with source URLs rather than relying solely on this summary overview.

# Claude Design: Key Capabilities

## Core Functions
Claude Design enables users to describe visuals and generate first drafts that stay on-brand, with refinement, sharing, and handoff capabilities.

## Handoff to Claude Code
Users can move seamlessly between Claude Design and Claude Code using `/design-sync` to pull design systems or `/design` to work directly within Claude Code sessions.

## Export Formats
The platform supports exporting to "PPTX, PDF, or HTML," with the ability to "hand off to Claude Code, or send to the apps you already use daily."

## Model Used
The page doesn't specify which Claude model powers Claude Design—this information isn't disclosed in the provided content.

## Availability
"Claude Design now works in every conversation with Claude." It's included in all plans, including the Free tier.

## Design System Setup
Teams can import systems from GitHub, design files, or raw uploads. Key feature: "Claude builds with your components, checks its output against your design system, and makes corrections before you see it."

## Design Variations
The platform includes "rich layout controls for quick visual and aesthetic shifts, including to drag, resize, and align elements directly" plus adjustment sliders for spacing and color refinement.

## Partner Integrations
Claude Design connects with Adobe, Canva, Gamma, Lovable, Miro, Replit, Vercel, and Wix for seamless workflow continuation.

# Design Tokens Format Module 2025.10 - Status

Yes, this is a stable final release. According to the document:

**Status:** "This specification is considered stable. Further updates will be provided in superseding specifications."

**Release Date:** 28 October 2025

**Classification:** Published as a Final Community Group Report (not a W3C Standard, but clarified as stable for implementation)

**Key Features:**

The specification establishes a JSON-based file format enabling interoperability between design tools, translation tools, and documentation platforms. Core capabilities include:

- **Token structure** with required `$value` properties and optional metadata (`$type`, `$description`, `$extensions`, `$deprecated`)
- **Hierarchical groups** for organizational flexibility
- **Group extension** via `$extends` property for inheritance and overrides
- **Token references** using curly brace syntax (`{group.token}`) and JSON Pointer notation
- **Predefined types:** color, dimension, fontFamily, fontWeight, duration, cubicBezier, number
- **Composite types:** strokeStyle, border, transition, shadow, gradient, typography
- **Property-level references** enabling fine-grained component reuse

The specification notably does NOT include a resolver module (that's a separate deliverable) and uses a standardized color representation rather than restricting to specific color spaces.

# Figma MCP Server Rate Limits

## Rate Limits by Plan and Seat

According to the documentation, here are the exact limits:

**Starter Plan & View/Collab Seats:**
- "Up to 20 per month"

**Professional Plan (Full/Dev seats):**
- "Up to 200 per day, 10 per minute"

**Organization Plan (Full/Dev seats):**
- "Up to 200 per day, 15 per minute"

**Enterprise Plan (Full/Dev seats):**
- "Up to 600 per day, 20 per minute"

Education plans match the Professional tier limits.

## Exempt Tools

Several tools don't count toward rate limits, including those that write data like `create_new_file` and `generate_figma_design`, plus the `whoami` tool.

## Access Requirements

You can only use the MCP server with files you already have access to. The documentation notes that permission errors typically stem from incorrect file links, using the wrong account, or lacking the required plan membership for the file's owner.

# Frontend Design Skill - Key Instructions

## Frontmatter Description
> Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.

## Core Directive
> **Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's.** This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: **make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.**

## Critical Aesthetic Warnings

The skill explicitly identifies five common AI-generated design defaults to **avoid**:

1. Warm cream backgrounds (#F4F1EA) + serif display + terracotta accent (#D97757)
2. Near-black background + bright acid-green/vermilion accent
3. Broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, dense columns
4. **SaaS-card kit**: identical rounded cards, uniform border-radius, soft grey shadows (rgba(0,0,0,.1)), gradient decorations
5. Template chrome: ALL-CAPS eyebrows, middle-dot metadata ('A · B · C'), spaced em dashes, tinted near-blacks, monospace data labels, arrow suffixes on links

## Two-Pass Design Process

**Pass 1 - Planning:**
- Color: 4–6 named hex values
- Type: typefaces and roles
- Layout: ASCII wireframes + alignment guidance
- Principles: uniqueness statement

**Pass 2 - Validation:**
> Review that plan against the brief before building: if any part reads like a generic default you would produce for any similar page, **revise that part, say what you changed and why.**

## Extremes to Employ
- **Ground designs in subject matter** (industry vernacular, materials, audience-specific aesthetics)
- **Typography as personality**: intentional typeface selection, clear type scale per Elements of Typographic Style
- **Avoid**: single-word highlights, ALL-CAPS labels, unnecessary typographic labels
- **Motion**: orchestrated single moments, not scattered fade-slide-up defaults
- **Written content**: conversational tone, active voice, no filler, each element does one job
